questions.prompt: Which principle is most useful when applying The @utility Directive?
options: shared tokens, utilities and component patterns should clarify rather than hide design decisions
It removes the need to understand HTML semantics, the CSS cascade or browser behavior.
It makes every interface responsive and accessible without testing.
It runs all utility classes as JavaScript in the browser.
questions.answer_key: shared tokens, utilities and component patterns should clarify rather than hide design decisions
questions.explanation: The @utility Directive is best understood through the syllabus topics: Defining a custom utility, Simple custom declarations, Complex custom utilities. Choose the technique deliberately and verify the result.

questions.prompt: Which workflow is strongest when working with the @utility directive?
options: Add classes until a screenshot looks acceptable without inspecting generated CSS.
Assume that starting a development server proves every page and state works.
Skip narrow-screen testing because utility-first CSS is automatically responsive.
document reusable classes and test their variants in a real component
questions.answer_key: document reusable classes and test their variants in a real component
questions.explanation: A reliable workflow checks generated CSS and the actual interface. Related topics include: Defining a custom utility, Simple custom declarations, Complex custom utilities, Reusing custom utilities.

questions.prompt: Which common mistake should you avoid when applying the @utility directive?
options: Use the official documentation for version-specific behavior.
Check keyboard states where controls are involved.
duplicating one-off values in many components increases design drift
Document intended behavior and test representative content.
questions.answer_key: duplicating one-off values in many components increases design drift
questions.explanation: Good styling work is verified, version-aware and tested with realistic content and input methods.
